core.text: To say what you go *to do*, Latin has **the supine (the special purpose form after a verb of going: dormītum it = goes to sleep)**: the participle stem with -um, used after *īre*, *venīre*, *mittere* and other verbs of moving: *ambulātum exit* — he goes out to walk; *salūtātum veniō* — I come to greet you. It can take an object like a verb: *amīcum salūtātum īvit*. Latin name: *supīnum*.
English uses a plain *to* here: *he went out to walk*, *they come to watch*.
Verb of motion + supine in -um = 'to do X'. A second supine in -ū follows facilis / difficilis: facile dictū — easy to say.

invented.en: The tired boys go to sleep.

core.text: *Salūtātum* is also the neuter of **the perfect participle (the 'having been done' word: laudātus = praised)**. Ask what it is doing: after a verb of going with no noun to agree with, it is the supine ('to greet'); agreeing with a noun (*oppidum salūtātum*) it is the participle.

teach.title: What it does
teach.say: Latin keeps one special form for saying what you go somewhere to do: **the supine (the special purpose form after a verb of going: dormītum it = goes to sleep)**. It answers that one question and no other: *Iūlius in cubiculum it dormītum* — Julius goes into the bedroom to sleep. It turns up only when somebody is going, coming, or being sent somewhere. There is a second supine as well, ending in *-ū*, and it does something else; that is step 3.

check.ask: Which word says what the boys are going into the garden for?

teach.title: How it is built, and that it never changes
teach.say: You already have it: it is the fourth dictionary form as it stands. *dormītum*, *lūsum*, *salūtātum*, *ēmptum*, *petītum*. It is not an adjective and agrees with nobody, so it looks the same whoever goes, and however many of them go.

teach.title: The other supine, in -ū
teach.say: There is a second form, ending in *-ū*, and it does something else: it finishes an adjective. *facile dictū*, easy to say; *difficile factū*, difficult to do. Like the first it never changes, not even beside a plural: *verba turpia dictū*.

teach.title: Supine, or participle?
teach.say: The *-um* supine and the neuter perfect participle are spelt alike, and that is the one real trap here. Ask what the word belongs to. A participle belongs to a noun and matches it: *librum lēctum*. A supine belongs to a verb of going and matches nothing at all: *vēnit dominum audītum*.

check.ask: *quaesītum* — is it describing a noun, or saying why the boy left?

teach.title: Using it
teach.say: The supine keeps whatever the verb governs, so it can bring its own object along: *aquam petītum*, *flōrēs carptum*, *patrem quaesītum*. Put the object first and the supine last, and the phrase reads as one piece of English: 'to fetch water'.

check.ask: *vocō, vocāre, vocāvī, vocātum*. Say what Aemilia goes out to do.

more.text: The learner's notes (week 22) call it the third verbal noun beside infinitive and gerund, with only two jobs: -um after motion for purpose, -ū to pin down an adjective. A deponent verb (passive-looking endings, active meaning: loquitur = he speaks) forms it the same way: *venī mēcum locūtum* — come and talk with me.

Ørberg (cap. XXII) lists everyday supines: *lavātum īre*, *dormītum īre*, *cubitum īre*. Supine + *īrī* makes the rare future passive infinitive (*laudātum īrī*, cap. XXIII). For purpose in general Latin prefers *ut* + subjunctive or *ad* + gerund; the supine stays with going and sending.
